review.title: A killed desktop dev server cannot leave a tracked file rewritten
review.acceptance: A desktop build or dev server cannot leave apps/web/next-env.d.ts rewritten in the working tree, under ANY termination. THE DEFECT, OBSERVED RATHER THAN PREDICTED, in round 81: the file was committed pointing at ./dist/desktop/dev/types/routes.d.ts instead of ./.next/types/routes.d.ts. Next regenerates that TRACKED file to name whichever distDir last built; the three *:desktop scripts snapshot and restore it around the child; and build-target.ts:300-342 already records that the restore happens ONLY ON NORMAL EXIT. Playwright signal-kills `next dev` when the harness finishes, so the rewrite survived, was staged by a routine `git add -A`, and was caught only by reading the diff before delivery. It typechecked locally because dist/desktop/dev happened to exist; on a fresh clone it would not have. REQUIRED: a forced termination -- SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGKILL of the child, and the parent being killed -- cannot leave the tracked file dirty. REQUIRED: THE SOLUTION MUST NOT DEPEND ON A NORMAL-EXIT CLEANUP HOOK ALONE. A second `process.on('exit')` handler is the same mechanism that already failed and would fail the same way under SIGKILL; the implementer must choose a design that is correct when no cleanup runs at all, and justify it. Two candidates, neither mandated: make the file untracked and generated (which changes what a fresh clone must do, and docs/DEVELOPMENT.md must then say so), or make the desktop distDir's type path stable so no rewrite occurs. REQUIRED: the regression is MECHANICALLY TESTED -- a test that starts a desktop invocation, kills it without letting it clean up, and fails if the tracked file differs from HEAD. A test that only exercises normal exit reproduces nothing, because normal exit already works. REQUIRED: the fix does not weaken the build-target split; build-target.test.ts must keep passing, including its assertion that no shipped module under apps/web/src names LIBERTY_BUILD_TARGET. NOT IN SCOPE: anything about product behaviour. This is a tooling defect and gpt-architect's ruling is explicit that it must not be folded into unrelated product work.
review.notes: Filed round 82 on gpt-architect's ruling item 4, which refused to let this stay a warning in a handoff. The scripts directory is named in allowedPaths because the three `node -e` wrappers inside apps/web/package.json are the thing that would move: JSON cannot carry a comment, which is why their reasoning currently lives in build-target.ts, and a real script file is the likeliest shape of the fix. It is not mandated -- the implementer chooses and justifies.

typecheck.evidence:
`npm run typecheck` -> "Tasks: 22 successful, 22 total", FULL TURBO. `npm run lint` -> 12/12, 0 errors. `npm run repo:validate` -> passed. `npm run ai:validate` -> valid.

THE TYPECHECK MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED THE DESIGN, and it is the one that makes untracking safe rather than merely idiomatic. The acceptance offers untracking as a candidate and warns it "changes what a fresh clone must do". Measured on this tree, twice:

  - `apps/web/next-env.d.ts` absent, `apps/web/.next/` absent -- the exact fresh-clone condition --
    `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/web/tsconfig.json` exits 0.
  - `next-env.d.ts` present but carrying the DESKTOP spelling, with `apps/web/dist/desktop/dev/`
    not existing, `tsc --noEmit` exits 0.

So a fresh clone typechecks with the file missing, and a developer whose last invocation was a desktop one typechecks with it stale. `tsconfig.json` lists the file under `include`, and an `include` entry that matches nothing is not an error -- only `files` is. Neither case needs a cleanup step, which is what lets the restore be deleted rather than hardened.

`node --check` is clean on both new scripts.

build.evidence:
`npx turbo run build --force` -> 12/12 tasks successful in 41s, no cache. `npm run build:desktop -w @liberty/web` -> exit 0 in 43s.

AND THE ASSERTION THAT MATTERS FOR THIS TASK, taken around the desktop build: the set of tracked files with uncommitted changes was captured before and after, and is IDENTICAL. The build did rewrite `apps/web/next-env.d.ts` -- it now reads `import "./dist/desktop/types/routes.d.ts"` -- and the tracked tree did not move, because git no longer tracks that file.

That is the whole shape of the fix in one measurement: the rewrite still happens, and it stopped mattering.

unit.evidence:
`npm run test` -> 22/22 turbo tasks; @liberty/web 1308, @liberty/persistence 268, @liberty/provider-sdk 288, @liberty/catalog-ingestion 152, @liberty/backend 36, all passing.

THE REGRESSION IS `scripts/test-desktop-target.mjs`, 9 assertions, ~10s, and it is wired into
`npm run test:scripts` so it actually runs. That wiring is the reason the root package.json joined
this task's surface: `scripts/` is not a workspace, `turbo run test` never visits it, and
`scripts/test-validate-repo.mjs` says so in its own header -- "a vitest suite placed here would be
written, committed, and never executed by any gate." The whole chain was run and every member
passes: validate-env 38 scenarios, ai-control-plane 71 scenarios, validate-repo 20 groups,
desktop-target 9 assertions, cloud dispatcher 35 scenarios.

WHAT THE REGRESSION ACTUALLY DOES, because the acceptance rules out the cheap version -- "a test
that only exercises normal exit reproduces nothing, because normal exit already works." Each of four
cases writes the WEB spelling into `apps/web/next-env.d.ts`, starts a real desktop dev server through
the wrapper in its own process group, WAITS UNTIL NEXT HAS REWRITTEN THE FILE to name the desktop
distDir, and only then kills it. The four terminations are the four the acceptance names: SIGTERM,
SIGINT and SIGKILL to the process group, and SIGKILL to the parent alone, which orphans the dev
server and is the case where no code of ours runs at all. After each, the set of tracked files with
uncommitted changes must equal a baseline captured at start.

THE NON-VACUITY CHECK IS PART OF THE TEST, not something I ran by hand: if the rewrite never happens,
the case FAILS with "this case proved nothing", rather than passing against a dev server that did not
start. Measured: the rewrite lands 1214 ms after spawn.

IT COMPARES AGAINST A BASELINE rather than demanding a clean checkout, because a developer running
`npm run test:scripts` mid-change has a dirty tree and a test that failed for that reason gets turned
off.

PROVEN NON-VACUOUS BY MUTATION, both directions:
  - `git add -f apps/web/next-env.d.ts`  -> 2 failed, 7 passed; the failure names the re-tracking and
                                            says why no cleanup hook can close it.
  - removing the `.gitignore` line       -> 1 failed, 8 passed.
  - restoring either                     -> 9 passed.

`build-target.test.ts` KEEPS PASSING as the acceptance requires, and it was UPDATED rather than left
alone because its old assertion encoded the implementation: it read the literal string
`LIBERTY_BUILD_TARGET:'desktop'` out of `scripts["build:desktop"]`, which was only true while the
one-liner was pasted into package.json. The test caught the change immediately -- "expected 'node
../../scripts/desktop-target.mjs…' to contain ..." -- and the replacement is strictly stronger: all
three `*:desktop` scripts must route through the one wrapper, the wrapper itself must set the
variable, and the plain `build` must contain neither. Three files covered where one was, and a
desktop script that quietly stopped routing through the wrapper is now a failure. Its other
assertion, that no shipped module under `apps/web/src` names the variable, is untouched and still
passes -- the wrapper lives in `scripts/`.

ONE DEFECT FOUND AND NOT FIXED HERE: `scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs` copies the repository per
scenario and its exclusion list misses `apps/desktop/sidecar`, the 196 MB packaged tree PW-0102
produces. With a packaged tree present the suite fills the disk and dies mid-copy -- observed as
`ENOSPC ... copyfile '.../apps/desktop/sidecar/node.exe'`. It is the same failure the list's own
`target` entry was added for. Unrelated to a killed dev server, so it is proposed separately rather
than folded in.

review.title: An option-looking event type is a usage error, not an event
review.notes: PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect RULING, round 93, and created unowned rather than claimed, on the PW-0501 precedent. Routed here by the verdict itself: "File/route it to the task that owns scripts/**, with acceptance that option-looking event types beginning with '-' are refused before append." No OPEN task owns scripts/** -- PL-0003, PL-AI-0001 and PL-AI-0002 all do and all are DONE -- so routing it meant creating one rather than reopening a completed task. SURFACE NOTE: scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs is included because the acceptance requires a test, and that suite is where the control plane's own behaviour is tested. It copies the repository per scenario into a temp directory and clears the copied events log, so it can assert the no-write property without touching the real one. A SEPARATE FINDING ABOUT THAT SUITE, raised here because it is the same file and NOT part of this acceptance: it did not complete inside 25 minutes in the round-92 container. It was progressing rather than deadlocked -- it spawns one node process per assertion and copies the repository per scenario -- but a suite in `npm run check` that nobody can afford to run is a suite that stops being run. ACCEPTANCE REPLACED in round 94 with gpt-architect's ruling. Two changes from the proposal: 'unchanged' became 'byte-identical', and a non-vacuity clause was added requiring valid event types to still append.

unit.evidence:
`node scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs` -> "AI control plane tests passed (72 scenarios)" (was 71; the new section is 10.5). The rest of the `test:scripts` chain also passes: validate-env 38 scenarios, validate-repo 20 assertion groups, desktop-target 9 assertions, cloud dispatcher 35 scenarios.

THE FIVE REQUIRED PROPERTIES, each measured against the LIVE CLI as well as in a fixture:

 - `event --help`, and any type beginning with `-`, is treated as usage input. Four spellings are
   covered in the test -- `--help`, `-h`, `--agent`, `-x` -- and each is refused with the message
   `Refused: "--help" looks like an option, not an event type, so nothing was appended to
   control/events.jsonl.` followed by the full command list.
 - THE REFUSAL OCCURS BEFORE APPEND. The check sits at the same call site as the existing empty-type
   check and runs before `event()`, which is the only function that writes.
 - `control/events.jsonl` IS BYTE-IDENTICAL after a refusal. Asserted with a Buffer comparison per
   case in the fixture, and checked against the real file here with `cmp` for both `event --help` and
   `event -x`: identical both times.
 - VALID TYPES STILL APPEND NORMALLY -- the acceptance's non-vacuity clause, "a fix that refused
   everything would satisfy every other line here". The test appends
   `control_plane.operator_error` and asserts exactly one new line with the message intact.
 - HISTORICAL JUNK AND ITS CORRECTIONS ARE UNTOUCHED. Nothing in this change reads or rewrites the
   log; the two `--help` events from round 93 and their corrections are still there, which is the
   point. "An audit log rewritten when it embarrasses its author is not an audit log."

ONE PROPERTY THE ACCEPTANCE DID NOT NAME AND THE TEST ASSERTS ANYWAY: a hyphen INSIDE a type is still
valid. The rule is about the first character, and refusing every hyphen would refuse
`operator.note-taken` -- a second defect wearing the first one's clothes. Covered explicitly.

THE EXIT CODE IS 2, not 0, and that is a judgement worth stating rather than burying: `event` was
asked to record something and recorded nothing, so a zero exit would let a wrapper script, or the
next person reading a terminal, believe an event was written. The usage text is printed either way,
because the person typing `--help` is asking for it.

The usage text was EXTRACTED into `printUsage()` rather than duplicated, so the refusal and the
unrecognised-command branch cannot drift apart. It is a function declaration, so it is hoisted above
the dispatch chain that calls it.

review.title: The documented migration command applies nothing and exits 0
review.notes: PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect RULING, round 93, created unowned rather than claimed, on the PW-0501 precedent. Found by PW-0312 while building a CI migration step and verified against a live database before being written down. SURFACE NOTE: `packages/persistence/migrations/**` covers both the journal and the SQL; `package.json` is included because the fix may be a change to the `db:migrate` script rather than to a data file, and that should not need a second amendment. `drizzle.config.ts` is a reviewDependency rather than writable: its `out` and `schema` settings decide where a journal would live, so a reviewer needs it in the window, but nothing here should need to change it. THE CI WORKAROUND SHOULD OUTLIVE THE FIX, and that is deliberate: the table count after the migration step is cheap and it is the assertion that would have caught this in the first place. ACCEPTANCE REPLACED in round 94 with gpt-architect's ruling, which is stronger than the proposal in three places: the impossibility regression, the non-zero exit on invalid metadata, and the condition on CI returning to the command. The proposal's original text is in the round-93 board.task_proposed event.

unit.evidence:
`npm run test` -> 22/22 turbo tasks. @liberty/persistence 268 tests (was 260; +8 from the new
`src/migration-journal.test.ts`), @liberty/web 1308, @liberty/backend 36, all passing. `npm run lint`,
`npm run typecheck`, `npm run repo:validate` all clean.

THE DEFECT, REPRODUCED HERE FIRST, against PostgreSQL 16.15 on a real connection string. Before the
fix, on a fresh empty database, `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence` left ZERO relations. One
correction to the record, because the exact failure shape decides what the regression has to assert:
on drizzle-kit 0.31.10 with NO journal the command exits **1**, not 0, and prints NOTHING on stderr --
a silent non-zero. The reported "exit 0, zero relations" is reproducible too, and it is the WORSE
neighbouring case: a journal that exists with `entries: []` prints "migrations applied successfully!",
exits 0, and creates nothing. Both are now impossible; I am recording the distinction rather than
repeating a measurement I did not make.

THE REPAIR, AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO. `drizzle-kit migrate` does not read a directory of
`.sql` files; it reads `meta/_journal.json` and applies the tags listed there. That directory held the
hand-written `0000_profile_scoped_identity.sql` and nothing else. The fix adds the missing metadata:
`migrations/meta/_journal.json` naming the existing file, and `migrations/meta/0000_snapshot.json`.
THE REVIEWED SQL IS BYTE-FOR-BYTE UNTOUCHED, which is the constraint gpt-architect set -- "Do not
silently generate a migration from today's schema if doing so would obscure the reviewed hand-written
migration's provenance." The snapshot was obtained by running `drizzle-kit generate` into a THROWAWAY
directory outside the repository and copying only `meta/0000_snapshot.json` across; the SQL that run
produced was discarded. The journal's `when` is 1787588559000 -- the author date of commit 1dd8e73,
which added the migration -- not the time this repair was typed.

THE SEVEN ACCEPTANCE ITEMS:
 1. fresh empty PostgreSQL database                  lib_final, 0 relations before
 2. the documented command                           `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence`
 3. it ACTUALLY CREATES the expected schema           exit 0, 8 tables: account,
                                                      active_profile_selection, playback_progress,
                                                      profile, session, user, verification,
                                                      watchlist_entry
 4. a second invocation is safely idempotent          exit 0, still 8 tables, drizzle ledger still 1 row
 5. NON-ZERO on invalid metadata or schema state      measured, four cases: no journal -> 1;
                                                      malformed journal JSON -> 1; journal tag with no
                                                      matching .sql -> 1; and the one that does NOT
                                                      fail, `entries: []` -> 0 with zero tables, which
                                                      is why item 6 asserts non-emptiness rather than
                                                      mere existence
 6. a regression proving the old behaviour impossible `src/migration-journal.test.ts`, 8 tests, and
                                                      PROVEN NON-VACUOUS by mutation: `entries: []`
                                                      turns 2 red, deleting the journal turns 7 red,
                                                      removing the snapshot turns 1 red, and restoring
                                                      each returns 8 green
 7. CI may return to the repaired command only after  NOT DONE HERE, and deliberately.
    that evidence exists                              `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is a reviewDependency
                                                      of this task, read-only. The evidence now exists;
                                                      the switch is proposed in the handoff.

THE EIGHT-TABLE POSTCONDITION IS KEPT, as required -- asserted in the test against the SQL so it runs
in the unit job without a database, and separately observed against the live one above.

TWO THINGS MEASURED THAT ARE WORTH THE RECORD. `db:check` is NOT a guard for this: with the journal
present and no snapshot it answered "Everything's fine". And a journal WITHOUT a snapshot makes the
next `db:generate` emit a duplicate migration re-creating all eight tables -- observed as
`0001_nervous_omega_red.sql` in a throwaway copy; with the snapshot installed the same command answers
"No schema changes, nothing to migrate". That is why the snapshot is part of the repair and why the
test asserts one per entry.

The five hand-written CHECK constraints survive the migration and are visible in the live database:
playback_progress_epoch_positive, playback_progress_position_non_negative,
playback_progress_position_within_runtime, playback_progress_runtime_positive,
playback_progress_seq_non_negative.

review.title: The sidecar half of the desktop contract was never wired into the server
review.acceptance:
PW-0101 designed the sidecar contract and PW-0102 built the shell that speaks it. NOTHING CONNECTED THE SIDECAR HALF. Three symptoms, all found in round 95 by starting the packaged artefact for the first time -- none is reachable by any existing test, because until the packaging corrective landed there was no packaged sidecar to start.

1. THE HANDSHAKE IS NEVER EMITTED. `lib/sidecar/handshake.ts` exports `formatHandshake` and `HANDSHAKE_PREFIX`; the only caller in the repository is its own test. The packaged server's complete stdout is Next's banner plus the catalog line -- no `liberty-sidecar-ready`. `shell.rs` waits for that line, times out, kills the child and reports `NoHandshake`. THE INSTALLED APPLICATION THEREFORE NEVER OPENS A WINDOW ON CONTENT.

2. THE EXPECTED HOST CANNOT MATCH. `sidecar.rs` sets LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST to BIND_HOST, the bare literal "127.0.0.1". `policy.ts`'s `authorizeRequest` compares it to the request's `Host` header with `!==`, and its comment requires exactness: "127.0.0.1:3000 and 127.0.0.1:3001 are different listeners". A Host header always carries a non-default port, so the comparison can never succeed. `policy.test.ts` uses "127.0.0.1:3100" -- an authority -- so the policy side expects host:port and the shell side sends a hostname. Each half is self-consistent; the pair is not.
   PROVEN BY A ONE-VARIABLE COMPARISON against the packaged tree: with "127.0.0.1" every route answered 403; with "127.0.0.1:<bound port>" /, /search, /profiles, /api/health and /title/<id> answered 200, the stylesheet 200 and a client chunk 200.

3. THE BIND-SAFETY GATE IS NOT WIRED IN. `checkBindSafety` refuses to start a sidecar that would bind 0.0.0.0 -- 'a sidecar inheriting a container's HOSTNAME would serve the whole network with a valid token that the user's own browser holds'. `proxy.ts` calls `readSidecarEnvironment` but NOTHING calls `checkBindSafety`. A written, tested security control that no code path reaches.

THE ORDERING PROBLEM THAT MAKES 2 NON-TRIVIAL, and the reason this needs a ruling rather than a patch: the expected host must contain the port, and BIND_PORT is "0" so the port does not exist until after the child binds. `handshake.ts` records why that was chosen -- the shell picking a port has a TOCTOU window and 'the user sees a blank window'. So either the sidecar derives its own authority after binding (a change in `lib/sidecar/**`), or the shell reserves a port (which reverses a reviewed decision), or the comparison changes shape (which its own comment argues against). ALL THREE ARE ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS; pick one deliberately.

REQUIRED: the packaged sidecar emits exactly one handshake line on stdout, and the shell reaches a window.
REQUIRED: a request from the shell's own WebView is AUTHORIZED, with the port question settled one way and the reasoning recorded.
REQUIRED: `checkBindSafety` is consulted before the listener accepts anything, and a sidecar that would bind non-loopback refuses to start.
REQUIRED: A TEST THAT COMPOSES THE TWO HALVES. Every one of these defects is a pair of self-consistent unit tests with nothing between them. Whatever form it takes -- a harness that starts the packaged server with the environment `plan_launch` produces and asserts an authorized request succeeds -- the property is that the shell's output and the sidecar's input are checked against each other rather than each against its own fixture.

NOT IN SCOPE: packaging (PW-0501), the Job Object, the launch token's minting, and anything requiring attended Windows hardware (PW-0103).
review.notes:
PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect RULING, round 95, created unowned rather than claimed, on the PW-0501 precedent. Found during PW-0501's qualification by starting the packaged sidecar -- the first time this project has run one. P0 because it is the difference between an installer that produces a working application and one that produces a window that never loads, and because PW-0603's certification sheet and PW-0103's experiment both sit downstream of a shell that can actually reach its own server.
SURFACE NOTE: spans apps/web/src/lib/sidecar/** and apps/desktop/src-tauri/, which is unusual and is the point -- the defect IS the seam between them, and a task confined to one side would reproduce the two-self-consistent-halves problem that caused it. PW-0501 currently holds apps/desktop/**, so these two must not be active at the same time; the overlap is real and is resolved by sequence, the same way PW-0102 and PW-0501 were.
WHAT PW-0501 STILL PROVES WITHOUT THIS: that CI produces an installer, that it installs and uninstalls, and that the packaged tree serves pages when given a correct environment. It has never claimed the application launches, and `.github/workflows/windows.yml` says so in its header.

typecheck.evidence:
`npm run typecheck` -> "Tasks: 22 successful, 22 total" (turbo, all packages). `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/web/tsconfig.json` exits 0 with no diagnostics after the final wording correction to `host_not_stated`. `npm run lint` -> "Tasks: 12 successful, 12 total", 0 errors; the single warning (`WatchlistEntryRow` unused in `in-memory-repository.test.ts`) predates this task and is outside its surface. `npm run repo:validate` -> "Project Liberty repository validation passed." `npm run ai:validate` -> valid, 106 tasks, 9 agents.

WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT IS THE POINT OF THE CHANGE: making `listeningPort` a REQUIRED third parameter of `authorizeRequest`, rather than one defaulted to null, turned "which call sites still judge a request without the port" into a compiler error. It found exactly one production call site (`apps/web/src/proxy.ts`) and ten test call sites. A defaulted parameter would have compiled, shipped, and silently judged every production request under the reduced contract.

unit.evidence:
`npm run test` -> 74 test files, 1308 tests, all passing (@liberty/web), 22/22 turbo tasks successful. The sidecar surface specifically: `npx vitest run apps/web/src/lib/sidecar/` -> 4 files, 63 tests passing -- policy.test.ts 33 (was 18), bootstrap.test.ts 14 (new), listener.test.ts 11 (new), handshake.test.ts 5 (unchanged).

THE REGRESSION PROPERTIES REQUIREMENT D ASKS FOR, EACH WITH THE FILE THAT HOLDS IT:
 1. the bind check runs on the real startup path and refuses a short token -- bootstrap.test.ts
 2. a refusal exits non-zero -- bootstrap.test.ts (every refusal case asserts exit [1])
 3. a refusal emits NO handshake -- bootstrap.test.ts
 4. the diagnostic names the variable and the minimum, and never the token value -- bootstrap.test.ts
 5. a hosted deployment is untouched: no check, no diagnostic, no exit, no handshake, no published port -- bootstrap.test.ts
 6. the handshake carries the ACTUAL bound port, never the requested PORT -- bootstrap.test.ts (PORT=0 in the environment, listener on 52341, asserts 52341 and asserts the line does not contain "port":0)
 7. exactly one handshake per process even when the startup path runs twice -- bootstrap.test.ts
 8. the handshake is the only line on stdout and carries the prefix the shell scans for -- bootstrap.test.ts
 9. the emitted line round-trips through `parseHandshake`, the parser the Rust side's contract is written against -- bootstrap.test.ts
10. the port is published for the request path BEFORE the line is printed -- bootstrap.test.ts
11. an ACTUAL non-loopback bind is refused even when the environment claimed loopback -- bootstrap.test.ts
12. an unestablishable or ambiguous bound port is a refusal, not a guess -- bootstrap.test.ts + listener.test.ts
13. sockets are not mistaken for listeners -- listener.test.ts (an outbound socket's ephemeral local port is the intermittent, production-only, under-load-only failure this prevents)
14. Host validation is hostname-exact: suffix, prefix, userinfo, 0.0.0.0, LAN, alternate loopback spellings and DNS names are all refused -- policy.test.ts
15. a malformed authority is refused rather than repaired: URL delimiters, whitespace, control characters, multi-colon unbracketed, non-decimal / out-of-range / zero-padded port, trailing dot, zone-scoped literal -- policy.test.ts
16. a Host naming the right hostname but a different port is refused when the port is known -- policy.test.ts
17. when the port is UNKNOWN the hostname and token are still enforced and the guard does not fall open -- policy.test.ts
18. a failing bind check refuses every request at the request boundary, closing the window between `listen()` and `exit(1)` -- policy.test.ts
19. one refusal shape for every failure, so the wire is not an oracle -- policy.test.ts (6 distinct failures, one JSON shape)
20. the port memo caches a hit and never a miss, so asking too early cannot freeze the answer to "unknown" -- listener.test.ts

Twenty, not sixteen; the extra four are 10, 13, 19 and 20, each of which is a failure mode found while implementing rather than one gpt-architect named.

review.title: PORT=0 never reaches the kernel: the packaged sidecar always tries to bind 3000
review.acceptance:
The packaged desktop sidecar binds a port the KERNEL chose, on 127.0.0.1, and reports it. Set by
gpt-architect's round-96 ruling; the twelve evidence items below are theirs, quoted in substance.

REQUIRED DIRECTION (theirs): keep the Next standalone output as the request handler; introduce the
smallest supported desktop-specific bootstrap that creates the HTTP listener explicitly on host
127.0.0.1 and port 0; read the actual port from server.address() after the listen callback; emit the
existing single handshake line with that port; preserve every PW-0105 control (per-launch token,
request authorization, Host validation, bind-safety, fail-closed, no LAN bind, no source-checkout
dependency); do not patch generated Next output after every build unless there is no stable supported
composition point; and if the public APIs cannot do it without unstable internals, STOP and document
the exact limitation before choosing another design.

FORBIDDEN, restated so a later round cannot reintroduce it: the shell must not probe for or preselect
a free TCP port. No portpicker. No bind-then-retry-higher loop.

ACCEPTANCE EVIDENCE, all twelve:
 1. launch with port 3000 deliberately occupied
 2. the packaged sidecar still starts successfully
 3. the actual listener port is not 3000 in that test
 4. the handshake contains the real bound port
 5. the shell parser accepts it
 6. all required routes serve successfully
 7. static / CSS / client assets load
 8. token and Host attack cases still fail
 9. non-loopback startup fails
10. nothing writes beside the executable
11. repeated launches can use different kernel-selected ports
12. no shell-side free-port probing exists
PLUS regression coverage "specifically preventing PORT=0 from silently becoming 3000 again".

AND A NINE-ITEM REPORT: bootstrap architecture chosen; whether only public/stable Next APIs are used;
exact proof with 3000 occupied; real bound port observed; handshake evidence; route/static/security test
results; Windows/Linux differences; commits; gate state; delivery bundle/apply script.
review.notes:
RULED BY gpt-architect IN ROUND 96 -- proceed, with the required direction in `acceptance`. The original
proposal notes are superseded by that ruling; what follows is what round 96 established empirically and
why the task has not started.

THE DEFECT, UNCHANGED. Next 16.3.1's generated standalone entry reads
`const currentPort = parseInt(process.env.PORT, 10) || 3000` and creates the server with
`allowRetry: false`. `parseInt("0", 10)` is `0`, which is falsy, so PORT=0 binds 3000 and gives up if it
is taken. Observed on the packaged sidecar with the shell's own environment:
`Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, exit 1.

THE DESIGN IS SETTLED AND PROVEN BY A WORKING PROTOTYPE. See the `research.api_limitation` event for the
full transcript. In short:
  - `next()` + `getRequestHandler()` are public and sufficient for the handler.
  - WE create the listener: `http.createServer(...)` then `listen(0, "127.0.0.1")`, and read
    `server.address().port`. The kernel chooses; nothing probes.
  - LISTEN FIRST, PREPARE SECOND, with the handler awaiting the `prepare()` promise. This is what makes
    PW-0105 need NO changes -- its instrumentation still runs after the bind, so its handle-table
    discovery and its handshake work unaltered -- and it also closes PW-0105 requirement A's residual
    window, because no request is served before the bind-safety check has run.
  - The ONE non-public coupling is `__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG`, set from
    `<distDir>/required-server-files.json`. `next({ conf })` is TYPED but silently ignored on the custom
    server path (`NextCustomServer.prepare` does not forward `conf` to `getRequestHandlers`), and the
    fully-public alternative -- a `next.config.js` in the packaged directory -- re-runs `assignDefaults`
    over an already-resolved config and measurably DROPS keys (`htmlLimitedBots`,
    `experimental.trustHostHeader`, and others). The implementation must assert at startup that the
    private variable took effect, so a future Next that removes it fails loudly.
  - Prototype result with 3000 occupied: two launches, ports 41623 and 40299, handshake correct both
    times, five routes 200, token/Host attacks 403.

WHY IT IS NOT STARTED: A SURFACE COLLISION WITH PW-0501, WHICH IS IN REVIEW.
The work needs `apps/desktop/sidecar-bootstrap/**` (new), `apps/desktop/scripts/package-sidecar.mjs`
(to lay the bootstrap and a layout file into the packaged tree) and
`apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/sidecar.rs` (so the shell spawns the bootstrap rather than Next's entry).
All three are inside PW-0501's `allowedPaths` (`apps/desktop/**`).

This is not a housekeeping objection. `reviewProblems` in `scripts/ai-control-plane.mjs` recomputes
PW-0501's fingerprint at HEAD and refuses DONE with "stale review: implementation under <surface> changed
after approval" whenever it differs from what was approved. So committing PW-0106 into `apps/desktop/**`
WOULD BLOCK PW-0501 FROM EVER REACHING DONE on gpt-architect's current approval -- whether that approval
lands before or after the commit. The control plane is right and the sequencing is real.

`dependencies: ["PW-0501"]` therefore holds this task until PW-0501 is DONE, which needs one thing:
gpt-architect's `architecture-review` on PW-0501 at 65a47d5. gpt's round-96 message says PW-0501 "may
proceed through REVIEW based on its Windows build/install evidence", which is a statement about its
lifecycle and NOT a gate result -- it names no commit and does not say APPROVED, so it was not recorded
as one.

IF gpt-architect would rather PW-0106 start first, the reversible alternative is to narrow PW-0501's
`allowedPaths` away from the three files above BEFORE approving it, so the two surfaces stop overlapping.
That is their call, not mine: it changes what an approval fingerprints.

recommended.title: The Drizzle snapshot names three primary keys the database does not have
recommended.acceptance: TO BE SET BY gpt-architect: which of the three remedies in the notes is taken is a ruling, not an implementation detail. Whatever is chosen must leave `npm run db:migrate` creating the same eight tables on a fresh database, must not alter the reviewed hand-written migration's SQL, and must come with an assertion that compares generated constraint names against a migrated database so the disagreement cannot return silently.
recommended.notes:
FOUND BY claude-backend WHILE REPAIRING PL-0406, PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect TO RULE ON. It is NOT
fixed there: PL-0406's acceptance says in terms that changing the schema and adding a second migration
are out of scope, and this needs one or the other.

THE FINDING, EXACT. PL-0406 installed `migrations/meta/0000_snapshot.json` so `drizzle-kit generate`
has a previous state to diff against -- without it the next `db:generate` emits a duplicate migration
re-creating all eight tables, which was measured. The snapshot is derived from the ORM schema in
`src/schema/index.ts`. Compared against the database the REVIEWED hand-written migration actually
produces, every foreign key and every unique constraint matches by name. THREE PRIMARY KEY NAMES DO
NOT:

  table                      live database name              snapshot expects
  active_profile_selection   active_profile_selection_pkey   active_profile_selection_session_id_pk
  playback_progress          playback_progress_pkey          playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk
  watchlist_entry            watchlist_entry_pkey            watchlist_entry_profile_id_content_id_pk

Measured against PostgreSQL 16.15: `pg_constraint` after `npm run db:migrate` on a fresh database,
against the `compositePrimaryKeys` keys in the installed snapshot.

WHY: the hand-written SQL writes `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL` and
`CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_pkey" PRIMARY KEY (...)`, so PostgreSQL uses its own `_pkey` convention
or the stated name. Drizzle's `primaryKey()` synthesises `<table>_<cols>_pk`. Both describe the same
KEY; they disagree only about what it is CALLED.

WHY IT MATTERS LATER RATHER THAN NOW. Nothing is broken today: the schema is correct, all eight tables
exist, the constraints are enforced, and `generate` diffs the ORM schema against the snapshot without
ever consulting the database. The trap is the first migration that touches a primary key. Drizzle
would emit `ALTER TABLE "playback_progress" DROP CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk"`,
which does not exist, and the migration would fail against every real database -- in whatever
environment it ran first.

THREE WAYS OUT, unranked, for the ruling:
  (a) Name the constraints in the ORM schema so the snapshot matches the database -- `primaryKey({ name:
      "playback_progress_pkey", columns: [...] })`. Smallest, changes no SQL, leaves the reviewed
      migration untouched. Changes the schema file, which PL-0406 could not.
  (b) A second migration that renames the three constraints to Drizzle's convention. Changes a live
      database to suit a tool's naming, which is the wrong way round.
  (c) Hand-edit the snapshot's three names. Cheapest and worst: a snapshot is generated output, and a
      hand-edit is lost the next time anyone regenerates it.

(a) looks right from here and is NOT being taken unilaterally, because it edits the schema module that
PL-0405 reviewed and because the choice is exactly the kind PL-0406's acceptance reserved.

WHAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT AND DID NOT: `npm run db:check` answers "Everything's fine" -- it validates
the journal, not the agreement between the snapshot and a real database. Whatever remedy is chosen
should come with an assertion that compares generated constraint names against a migrated database, or
this recurs the next time a snapshot is produced.
